result.summary: Hesiod describes the house of Hades guarded by a hound, then the goddess Styx and the oath the gods swear by her water. He then tells of the edges of the world, the Titans' prison, and Zeus's battle against the monster Typhoeus, whom he defeats and hurls into Tartarus.

scenes.title: The Hall of Hades
scenes.summary: The halls of Hades and Persephone are guarded by a hound that fawns on entrants but devours any who try to leave.
scenes.stakes: Anyone entering the house of Hades can never leave again without being devoured.

scenes.title: Styx and the Great Oath
scenes.summary: Styx lives apart in her silver-pillared house. Iris fetches her water for the gods' oath, and a god who swears falsely is cast out for nine years.
scenes.stakes: A god forsworn lies breathless for a year and is excluded from the gods for nine more.

scenes.title: Edges of the World
scenes.summary: The sources and ends of earth, Tartarus, sea and heaven lie together, with bronze gates. The Titans dwell beyond, while Cottus, Gyes and Briareos live by Ocean.

place.name: Tartarus and the edge of the earth

scenes.title: Zeus Defeats Typhoeus
scenes.summary: Earth bears the hundred-headed Typhoeus, who would have ruled all had Zeus not noticed. Zeus thunders, strikes him down, scorches the earth, and casts him into Tartarus.
scenes.stakes: Zeus's rule over gods and mortals is threatened by Typhoeus.

alias_notes.explanation: Epithet used here for the god who makes Briareos his son-in-law; elsewhere usually a title of the sea god, so the identification is uncertain.

notable_quotes.reason: Memorable description of the hound that lets all in and none out.
Dramatic turning point: Typhoeus nearly overthrows Zeus.

analysis.text: The passage shows Zeus's rule secured against the last great challenge, and the oath of Styx as the guarantee of divine order.
The Typhoeus tale likely echoes older Near Eastern storm-god combat myths, such as Hittite and Babylonian dragon-slaying stories.

legacy.text: The hound at the gates of Hades is Hesiod's early picture of Cerberus, a figure used by later poets such as Virgil and Dante.
Typhoeus, as Typhon, gave later tradition the idea of monsters buried under volcanoes, and the word typhoon is sometimes linked to him.

fun_facts.text: The oath by the water of Styx remained proverbial; later writers made it the most binding oath even for Zeus.

language_notes.text: "The god of the lower-world" is Hades, ruler of the dead; his name also names his realm. Persephone is his queen.
"Suffers them not" is archaic for "does not allow them"; "whomsoever" means any person at all.
"Back-flowing" describes Ocean as a river circling the world and flowing back into itself. The "1623" is a stray footnote marker.
"Beetling" means overhanging or jutting out, describing the cliff from which Styx's water drips.
"The main" means the open sea. The "1624" is a stray footnote marker.
"Forsworn" means having sworn falsely; "libation" is a liquid poured out as an offering. "Ambrosia and nectar" are the gods' food and drink.
"Penance" here means punishment or suffering imposed for the offence, not a voluntary act of repentance.
The same cosmic roots and boundaries were described earlier in the poem, near the Titans' prison; Tartarus is the dark pit beneath the earth.
"The deep-roaring Earth-Shaker" is Poseidon, named only by epithet; he makes Briareos his son-in-law.
"Bare" is an archaic past tense of "bear"; "of the love of Tartarus" means by union with Tartarus.
"A thing past help" means an irreparable disaster, one that no one could have remedied.
"Crucibles" are heat-proof pots in which metals are melted.

context_notes.text: The hound is Cerberus, named elsewhere in the poem, guardian of the underworld gates.
Iris is the gods' messenger and goddess of the rainbow. Her father Thaumas is a sea-god.
Zeus is king of the gods. Swearing by Styx was the most binding oath, which even gods could not break without penalty.
The Titans are the older generation of gods, defeated by Zeus and the Olympians and confined in the gloom below.
Cottus, Gyes and Briareos are the hundred-handed giants who helped Zeus defeat the Titans.
Zeus's thunderbolt, lightning and thunder are his signature weapons, given to him earlier in the poem.
Hephaestus is the god of the forge and metalworking, so his name stands for fire used in smithing.

literary_notes.text: The dog's friendly fawning welcome hides its deadly purpose, making the hospitality a trap.
The rock vault and silver pillars rising to heaven give Styx's dwelling a grand, remote look that matches her awesome status.
Calling the tenth stream "a sore trouble to the gods" presents the water as a source of pain, foreshadowing the punishment for perjury.
Repeating "nine years" at the sentence's end stresses the length and severity of the exile.
Flickering tongues and flashing fire from the eyes create a vivid, terrifying picture of the monster.
The near-disaster conditional builds suspense and prepares for Zeus's decisive intervention.
The whole earth, sky and sea seething conveys the cosmic scale of the battle.
Melting earth is compared to tin and iron in a smith's fire, making the scale of the scorching understandable through craft.
"Wide Tartarus" stresses the pit's vastness, a fitting prison for the monster.
